George III. King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until his death in 1820. His long reign was marked by global conflicts, including the Seven Years' War and the Napoleonic Wars. Yet he is best remembered for presiding over the loss of the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War, when the thirteen colonies declared independence from his crown.

George's reign also saw the formal unification of Great Britain and Ireland through the Act of Union in 1800, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In his later years, however, George suffered from severe, recurring mental illness that would eventually become permanent. The nature of his condition remains debated by historians, though some have hypothesized it was porphyria. His illness inspired the famous play and film The Madness of King George, capturing the tragedy of his gradual incapacity.

Due to his complete mental incapacity, his eldest son ruled as Prince Regent starting in 1811, initiating the Regency era that would define the architecture and culture of the time. George was nicknamed Farmer George because of his keen interest in agriculture, farming, and simple domestic life, a hobby that provided him respite from the burdens of kingship. His son George IV would succeed him on the throne, while his granddaughter Victoria would go on to become one of Britain's greatest monarchs, inheriting an empire George had struggled to maintain.
